source: Rivera et al. (2024) Escalation Risks from Language Models in Military and Diplomatic Decision-Making
finding: Five off-the-shelf LLMs played nation agents in a scenario-driven wargame. All escalated, often suddenly, with arms races and rare nuclear use. No clear pattern.
numbers: 5 models (GPT-4, GPT-4-Base, GPT-3.5, Claude 2.0, Llama-2-Chat-70b); 3 start scenarios (neutral, invasion, cyberattack); 8 nation agents; 14 simulated days; 10 runs per condition; some runs changed escalation score by more than 50% in one turn.
limits: Fixed menu of 27 actions; world model summarised by GPT-3.5; GPT-4-Base (no RLHF) escalated most. A scenario simulator, not a test of scenario-planning method.
agent_relevance: A model asked to play out a scenario drifts toward drama and escalation. Any scenario step in our agent must be checked by code, not trusted as a forecast.

source: Lamparth et al. (2024) Human vs. Machine: Behavioral Differences Between Expert Humans and Language Models in Wargame Simulations
finding: LLM-simulated teams agree with 214 national-security experts at a high level but differ in specific moves and strategy. Simulated team talk is short, harmonious and unrealistic.
numbers: 214 experts in 48 teams; US-China crisis; GPT-3.5, GPT-4, GPT-4o. Of 21 possible actions, GPT-3.5 matched human frequency on 16, GPT-4 on 10, GPT-4o on 9. Player background (profession, gender, age) changed nothing significant.
limits: One fictional scenario; US-biased expert sample. Whether the LLM simulated a discussion or answered directly changed aggressiveness.
agent_relevance: Role-played stakeholder debate inside one model is mostly agreement, not real diversity (supports G4). Do not count simulated voices as independent views.

source: Lamparth et al. (2024), instruction test inside the wargame study
finding: When the President's three priorities were added to the briefing, models changed behaviour in model-specific ways. GPT-3.5 became more likely to fire at Chinese vessels and to use the AI weapon fully automated.
numbers: Priorities: protect service members, limit carrier damage, avoid escalation. GPT-4 only dropped 'Hold fire' options; GPT-4o dropped only 'Hold fire unless fired upon'. Move two: no significant difference for any LLM.
limits: Exact deltas are in the paper's appendix C and were not recorded here.
agent_relevance: Stated goals do not reliably steer scenario play. Constraints need code-side checks.

source: Lamparth et al. (2024), length of simulated dialogue
finding: More simulated dialogue raised aggressiveness toward the human level for GPT-3.5 and GPT-4, but raised the number of chosen actions above human levels for all models.
numbers: Dialogue varied in chunks of about 350 words; aggressiveness = aggressive actions minus de-escalatory actions.
limits: Suggests post-hoc reasoning: the output depends on how much text is generated first.
agent_relevance: Prompt length and format are a hidden knob on scenario output. Fix them and log them.

source: Elbaum and Panter (2025) Managing Escalation in Off-the-Shelf Large Language Models
finding: Partial replication of Rivera's neutral wargame with Mistral-7B. Low temperature and a short reflection prompt cut escalation a lot.
numbers: 10 runs per treatment. Temperature 1 to 0.5: -38% escalation; to 0.01: -48%. Reflection (planning) prompt: -28%. Reflection (de-escalation) prompt: -57%. Final-day escalation: -40% (temperature 0.01) and -42% (de-escalation prompt). Extra prompt text under 50 words on a 1800-word prompt.
limits: One small model, one scenario, no RLHF. The de-escalation prompt tells the model what answer is wanted, so it may be steering, not insight. Authors are a policy group.
agent_relevance: Scenario output is very prompt-sensitive. A reflection step that cites relevant theory is cheap, but a steering prompt changes the answer by design, so G1 says use it only on a signal.

source: Jensen et al. (2025) Critical Foreign Policy Decisions (CFPD) Benchmark
finding: Seven LLMs answered 400 expert-written scenarios in four domains. Models differ a lot in escalation and show country bias.
numbers: 7 models; 400 scenarios (Elbaum cites 66,000 question-answer pairs). Qwen2 72B, Gemini 1.5 Pro-002 and Llama 3.1 8B gave significantly more escalatory advice than Claude 3.5 Sonnet and GPT-4o. All models advised less escalation for China and Russia than for the US and UK.
limits: Abstract and Elbaum's summary read; the full paper was not read. Temperature 0 throughout.
agent_relevance: Which model runs the scenario step changes the outcome. Actor identity in the prompt biases the advice, so label actors neutrally.

source: Li, Li and Zhou (2026) When AI Navigates the Fog of War
finding: Frontier models reason about an ongoing 2026 conflict after their training cutoff. They read incentives and constraints well but are less reliable on ambiguous multi-actor politics. Their narratives drift over time.
numbers: 11 temporal nodes, 42 node-specific questions, 5 general questions. Models include claude-sonnet-4.6, gpt-5.4, gemini-3.1-flash, Qwen. Models gave point probabilities, for example 80% to 95% for Iranian retaliation.
limits: Qualitative analysis. The conflict was unresolved at writing, so no ground-truth accuracy score. Models showed early over-expectation of rapid containment.
agent_relevance: A clean way to test scenario reasoning without hindsight leakage. Weak spot: multi-actor politics, where our agent should lean on code checks and base rates.

source: Halawi et al. (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models
finding: Plain models forecast poorly. A system with news retrieval, reasoning prompts, fine-tuning and ensembling nears the human crowd.
numbers: Test questions from after June 1, 2023; 5 platforms. Brier scores: random 0.250, human crowd 0.149, best plain model (GPT-4-1106) 0.208, their system 0.179; accuracy 71.5% vs crowd 77.0%. Better than crowd in some settings (crowd uncertain, early retrieval). GPT-4 gave 0.01 to 0.03 lower Brier than other base models.
limits: Binary questions only. Forecasting, not scenarios. System still trails the crowd overall.
agent_relevance: Scenarios give branches; forecasting scores them. Retrieval plus ensembling is the measured route. Require probabilities to be scored against outcomes, not narrated.

source: Liu et al. (2024) DeLLMa: Decision-Making Under Uncertainty with LLMs
finding: A four-step scaffold (enumerate unknown states, forecast their probabilities, elicit utility, take expected utility) beats plain and chain-of-thought prompting. It is a scenario-analysis pipeline written as code.
numbers: Up to +40% decision accuracy versus competing methods; gains grow with number of actions. Agriculture: 7 fruits, 120 decision instances from a USDA report. Human agreement with DeLLMa state forecasts about 65 to 70% across three LLMs; annotation agreement 77.5%. Test-time scaling helped (sample sizes 4 to 64).
limits: Two domains (agriculture, stocks); gains weaker on stocks, blamed on volatile data. Costly in calls.
agent_relevance: Closest working analogue of scenario planning in an agent loop: state enumeration plus code-computed expected utility (matches G5). Worth a test.

source: Liu et al. (2024) DeLLMa, stocks and o1 comparison
finding: On stock decisions DeLLMa gains were smaller. Per the text, a large sampled DeLLMa could beat zero-shot o1-preview.
numbers: Agreement with human labels: agriculture 73.3%, stock 64.2% (as read from a layout-extracted table). DeLLMa with 64 samples and 25% overlap outperformed o1-preview zero-shot per the text.
limits: Table cells were read from layout-extracted text and may be misaligned; treat the table figures as approximate.
agent_relevance: Structure can match a stronger model on uncertainty tasks, but only where data are not very noisy.

source: Wang et al. (2024) K-Level Reasoning with Large Language Models
finding: Recursive 'what would they think I think' reasoning (a competitor-move step like scenario war-gaming) beat prompting baselines in dynamic games.
numbers: Guess-0.8-of-the-average game: win rate 0.65 for K-Level Reasoning versus lower for other methods (0.16 to 0.42 in the same row); average survival round 9.01 in the auction game; 59.08% win rate in a further setting. Going to K=3 lowered win rate in one game.
limits: GPT-based players, toy games with known payoffs. Deeper levels did not always help.
agent_relevance: Competitor-reaction steps help only up to a point. Depth should be capped.

source: Fu et al. (2024) DeFine: Decision-Making with Analogical Reasoning over Factor Profiles
finding: Builds probabilistic factor profiles from 800+ company earnings-call transcripts and retrieves similar past cases, improving buy/sell calls over the DeLLMa baseline.
numbers: Stock labels: strong sell below -5%, sell -5 to -2, hold -2 to +2, buy +2 to +5, strong buy above +5. Class mix: strong buy 34%, buy 15%, hold 21%, sell 9%, strong sell 21%. Gains reported on strong buy, buy, hold and sell classes.
limits: Exact accuracy numbers not recorded here; one data type.
agent_relevance: Analogy to past cases plus explicit factor weights is a scenario-lite pattern. Measure whether retrieval brings real gain over plain prompts.

source: Lee et al. (2024) PlanRAG: Plan-then-Retrieval Augmented Generation for decision making
finding: An LLM that first writes an analysis plan, retrieves data, and re-plans on failure beats iterative RAG on strategy-game decision questions.
numbers: +15.8% in the Locating scenario and +7.4% in Building over iterative RAG. Removing re-planning cut accuracy by 10.8 points (Locating) and 0.9 (Building). Questions come from Europa Universalis IV and Victoria 3.
limits: Game databases, not real firms.
agent_relevance: Re-planning after a failed check (G1-style) is the part that helped. Supports revising from real output.

source: Business Arena (2026) Benchmarking LLM Agents in a Realistic Marketplace
finding: 15 frontier agents ran a simulated cross-border shop. Results vary ninefold; many runs lose money; human-designed strategies beat every model.
numbers: Mean final net worth $20,856 to $188,488 (9.0x). 51% of runs lose money; only 4 models kept starting capital in every trial. Best expert strategy $436,195, more than twice the best model mean. Ten runs per model.
limits: Single simulated world built by the authors.
agent_relevance: Open-ended business operation under uncertainty is still far from human strategy. Adds caution on adoption, as with scenario-planning claims.

source: Business Arena (2026) skill-level analysis
finding: Models show recognisable operating styles: under-investing shops (22.3% of capital deployed), margin-focused sellers (52.0% margin), volume wholesalers (sell-through above 93%), stranded shops (12.1% margin, under 40% sold).
numbers: Capital utilisation up to 199% for the best models. One weak model priced every item with a single rule.
limits: Descriptive, not a causal test of any prompt or scaffold.
agent_relevance: Failure modes are idle capital and ignored margin, not lack of ideas. This echoes the de Geus audit: weak follow-through, not the scenarios.

source: KWBench (2026) Unprompted problem recognition in knowledge work
finding: Models fail to recognise what kind of problem a business situation is when not told. They pass few tasks, then produce polished output on the wrong problem.
numbers: 223 tasks (acquisitions, negotiations, incentive design and more); 16 models; best model passes the mandatory gate on 27.9%; top two agree on only 31.7% of passes; routing across the top 8 covers 50.7%; models scoring zero still meet about half the optional criteria; the same models explain the game-theory concept when asked directly.
limits: Authors' own rubric; conjunctive scoring is strict. Author list not checked.
agent_relevance: Strongest hint against trusting an LLM scenario step: it may frame the wrong problem fluently. Add a problem-framing check before scenarios.

source: Chen et al. (2024) How far can we extract diverse perspectives from LLMs
finding: Criteria-based prompting raises coverage of distinct viewpoints over plain sampling, but coverage stays below human diversity.
numbers: One recall figure read: 37.5% on CHEM-101 statements (N = 20); other figures not extracted.
limits: Subjective-opinion tasks, not scenarios; numbers partial.
agent_relevance: Scenario sets need varied axes defined in code (criteria), not 'give me four scenarios'.

source: Wong et al. (2024) SimpleStrat: Diversifying Language Model Generation with Stratification
finding: Raising temperature lowers quality and does not give coverage of valid answers. Having the model split the answer space into strata, then sampling one stratum, gives better coverage.
numbers: Recall +0.05 over GPT-4o; average KL divergence reduced by 0.36 versus Llama 3 (CoverageQA).
limits: Underspecified questions with many valid answers; not scenario quality. Author names not verified.
agent_relevance: A method to generate different futures: stratify first (axes), then draw. Fits scenario axes without extra voters.

source: Anonymous (2026) Are We Measuring Strategy or Phrasing? Surface- vs approach-level diversity
finding: Common diversity metrics measure wording, not approach. Diversity-aware training kept surface scores while approach diversity fell.
numbers: Human-calibrated LLM judge framework; math reasoning tasks.
limits: Math domain; numbers not extracted.
agent_relevance: If we score scenario sets for diversity, judge distinct causal logic, not distinct phrasing.

source: What-If Analysis of Large Language Models (WiA-LLM) (2025)
finding: Training a model as a language-based world model for what-if prediction improved forecasting of game-state changes and expert-like play.
numbers: 74.2% accuracy forecasting game-state change (27 points above base model) in Honor of Kings.
limits: Needs fine-tuning and RL, unlike our no-training constraint. MOBA game, not business.
agent_relevance: Predicted outcomes can be scored against real next states; our version must use code-checkable outcomes.

source: Wong (2025) Speculative futures of education: scenarios from ChatGPT, Gemini and DeepSeek
finding: Three chatbots wrote utopian and dystopian education scenarios. Themes were shared (equity, control), and AI appeared as a central driver.
numbers: 3 chatbots: GPT-4o, Gemini 2.0 Flash, DeepSeek R1; qualitative, no counts in the abstract.
limits: Abstract read from the Crossref record only; full text paywalled. Exploratory, no human baseline.
agent_relevance: Models share blind spots and put AI at the centre. Correlated error across vendors (G4).

source: Kozachek (2026) Entering the age of hybrid futures: a comparative study of human and GPT-generated scenarios
finding: A Futures-journal study compares human-written and GPT-generated scenarios. Seen as a title only.
numbers: No numbers obtained.
limits: Publisher page gave only a redirect; abstract and full text not read.
agent_relevance: Most direct human-vs-LLM scenario comparison found; high-priority follow-up.

source: McIntosh (2026) Linking generative AI and morphological analysis to conduct foresight evaluation
finding: ChatGPT 4o scored a 1976 Hudson Institute scenario report against today's world. The second-most-pessimistic scenario fitted best.
numbers: Best fit 88% (second-most-pessimistic); most optimistic scenario worst at 40%. Four views by ten issues.
limits: Abstract only (Crossref). One report, one model, no human check of the grader.
agent_relevance: LLMs can speed retrospective scoring of old scenarios, but the grader needs an outside check (G5).

source: Morozumi and Hayashi (2026) LLM-Based Risk Scenario Generation for Hardware Products
finding: Generates risk scenarios with an LLM and validates them against real user reviews.
numbers: No abstract or numbers retrieved.
limits: Title only; not opened.
agent_relevance: A rare check of LLM scenarios against real outcomes. Follow up.

source: Rosen (2025) Problems with creating useful scientifically valid futures scenarios (Futures)
finding: A critique of scenario validity in futures work. Seen only as a title.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Not opened; paywalled.
agent_relevance: Fits the caution on adoption: scenario usefulness is hard to show.

source: Search note for this angle (no single source)
finding: No study was found that tests Shell-style scenario planning itself (plan with scenarios vs without) on language models. Only neighbouring work exists: wargame simulators, decision pipelines, forecasting.
numbers: WebSearch budget was exhausted; arXiv, Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex APIs were rate limited. Papers were found through Hugging Face paper search and Crossref.
limits: Coverage gap likely. Recheck arXiv for scenario planning, strategic foresight and futures once limits clear.
agent_relevance: Treat scenario planning as untested for LLM agents. Adopt only pieces with measured gain: state enumeration with code-computed utility, re-planning on failure, stratified generation.
